title: Rebuild a Line From Taller-Ahead Counts
statement:
People were standing in a single-file line, and then got shuffled. You get the list people, where people[i] = [h, k]: the person's height h, and k, the number of people standing in front of them in the original line whose height was greater than or equal to h.

Rebuild the original line and return it as a list of [h, k] pairs from front to back. The input always describes a real line, and that line is unique.

examples.why: The 3 has one taller person (5) in front. The 4 has two (5 and 6); the 3 in front of it is shorter and does not count.
Equal heights count: the second 2 sees one person of height ≥ 2 in front.
One person is a line of one.

constraints: The input comes from a real line
hints: Who is easiest to place: the shortest person or the tallest? Whose k depends on whom?
Shorter people are invisible to a taller person's k. So if you place people from tallest to shortest, inserting someone later never changes the counts of those already placed.
Sort by height descending (ties: smaller k first). Insert each person at index k of the list built so far; exactly k people already there are at least as tall.

explain.intuition:
A person's k only counts people at least as tall as them. So shorter people are invisible to taller ones. If you seat everyone from tallest to shortest, each new person is shorter than (or equal to) everyone already seated, so everyone already in the line counts toward their k, and putting them anywhere does not change anyone else's count.

That makes the placement forced: the new person must have exactly k people in front of them, so insert them at index k. Among equal heights, place the smaller k first; the person with the larger k then correctly sees the earlier one in front.
steps: Sort by height descending; for equal heights, by k ascending.
For each person in that order, insert them at index k.
pitfalls: Sorting equal heights by k descending. Then a later insertion at a smaller index pushes an equal-height person back and breaks their count.
Counting only strictly taller people. Equal heights count too.
Expecting O(n log n) from array insertion. Each insert shifts elements, so this is O(n²); fine for n = 2000. A Fenwick tree finds the k-th free slot in O(log n) if you need more.

solutions.title: Shortest first into empty slots
solutions.idea: Sort ascending by height (ties: larger k first). Each person goes into the (k + 1)-th still-empty slot, because every slot left empty will later hold someone at least as tall.

solutions.title: Tallest first, insert at index k
solutions.idea: Shorter people never affect a taller person's count, so seat from tallest to shortest and insert each person exactly k places from the front.

followups: Make it O(n log n) for n = 10⁶. Which structure finds the k-th empty slot quickly?
The input may be inconsistent. How would you detect that no line matches?
